quick_notes.title: Angle of Elevation
quick_notes.explanation: The angle of elevation is the angle you make when you look up from a straight, flat line in front of you, called the horizontal line, to see an object that is above that line. For example, if you stand on the ground and look up at the top of a tree, the angle between your flat forward gaze and your upward gaze is the angle of elevation. This angle is always measured from the horizontal line upward, so it can only be between 0 degrees (looking straight ahead) and 90 degrees (looking straight up). To solve problems with this angle, you use a right triangle where the horizontal line is one side, the vertical height of the object is the other side, and your line of sight to the object is the slanted side, called the hypotenuse. You then use the tangent ratio, which compares the opposite side (the height) to the adjacent side (the distance from you to the object), to find the missing height or distance.

quick_notes.title: Angle of Depression
quick_notes.detail: Looking DOWN from horizontal line. Equal to angle of elevation from the object due to alternate interior angles.
quick_notes.explanation: The angle of depression is the angle you measure when you look down from a straight, level line of sight, like looking from your eyes straight out to the horizon. To find it, you imagine a horizontal line (a flat, level line) going out from your eyes, and then you measure the angle between that horizontal line and your line of sight as you look down at an object below you. This angle is always equal to the angle of elevation, which is the angle you would measure if you were standing at that object and looking up at you, because these two angles are formed by a pair of parallel horizontal lines and the same slanted line of sight, creating what are called alternate interior angles.

quick_notes.title: The 45-45-90 Triangle
quick_notes.detail: Ratio of sides (Base : Perp : Hyp) : 1 : 1 : sqrt(2).
quick_notes.explanation: The 45-45-90 triangle is a special type of right triangle where the two smaller angles are each 45 degrees, making the two legs equal in length. Because the two legs are equal, the ratio of the side lengths is always 1 to 1 to the square root of 2, meaning if the base and perpendicular are each 1 unit long, the hypotenuse is the square root of 2 units long. The hypotenuse, which is the side opposite the 90-degree angle, is always the longest side and is found by multiplying either leg by the square root of 2. For example, if one leg is 5, the other leg is also 5, and the hypotenuse is 5 times the square root of 2.

quick_notes.title: The 30-60-90 Triangle
quick_notes.detail: Ratio of sides (Side opp to 30 : Side opp to 60 : Hyp) : 1 : sqrt(3) : 2.
quick_notes.explanation: The 30-60-90 triangle is a special right triangle, meaning a triangle with one 90-degree angle, that has angles of 30 degrees, 60 degrees, and 90 degrees. The sides of this triangle always follow a fixed ratio, which is a way of comparing their lengths to each other. The side opposite the 30-degree angle is the shortest, and its length is called 1 unit. The side opposite the 60-degree angle is longer, and its length is the square root of 3, which is about 1.732, times that same unit. The hypotenuse, which is the longest side opposite the 90-degree angle, is exactly 2 times that same unit. So if you know the length of the shortest side, you can find the other two sides by multiplying that length by the square root of 3 for the side opposite 60 degrees, and by 2 for the hypotenuse.

quick_notes.title: Multi-triangle problems
quick_notes.detail: Moving towards or away from an object. Use the tangent ratios of both angles and equate the height.
quick_notes.explanation: Multi-triangle problems involve two different right-angled triangles that share the same vertical height, like when you are moving towards or away from a tall object such as a building or a tree. The tangent ratio, often written as tan, is a way to compare the opposite side of an angle to the adjacent side in a right triangle, and you use it for both angles given in the problem. For example, if you first stand far away and measure the angle of elevation to the top of a building, then walk closer and measure a new angle, you have two triangles with the same height but different distances. To solve, you set the height equal in both triangles by writing the height as the distance times the tangent of the angle for each triangle. This gives you an equation where you can solve for the unknown distance or height, because the height is the same in both expressions.
